   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

Read the result before you start the task anew or do it here: after "Not withdrawn", do neither.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session
tools.description: Move the task you are in the middle of into its own session (a fork of this conversation plus your remaining plan) so you can answer the user now. Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

import { expect, test as setup } from "@playwright/test"
import { mkdir } from "node:fs/promises"

const authFile = "test-results/.auth/forge-owner.json"

setup("authenticate through the real credentials flow", async ({ page }) => {
  setup.setTimeout(150_000)
  const password = process.env.ADMIN_E2E_PASSWORD
  if (!password) throw new Error("ADMIN_E2E_PASSWORD is required.")

  await page.goto("/login")
  await page.getByLabel("Email", { exact: true }).fill("forge-owner@example.test")
  await page.getByLabel("Password", { exact: true }).fill(password)
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Sign in", exact: true }).click()
  await page.waitForURL(/\/(dashboard|command-centre)$/, { timeout: 90_000 })
  await expect(page.locator("#admin-main-content")).toBeVisible()
  await expect(page.getByRole("navigation")).toBeVisible()

  await mkdir("test-results/.auth", { recursive: true })
  await page.context().storageState({ path: authFile })
})

content.text:
I've paused the deploy because the server has stopped responding. Nothing on production has changed: no migrations, no new build, no PM2 cutover.

**What happened**
- **Server down:** from about 09:01 UTC, SSH, HTTPS and ping to the server all time out. scalesmiths.co.uk shows Cloudflare's 522 error, meaning Cloudflare can't reach the server, so the live site is down for everyone, not just me. The only thing I ran just before was a database backup, which failed on its first query and was reading a 21 MB database at most. That shouldn't take a server down, so I suspect a problem on the hosting side. Please check the VPS provider's console, or reboot it from there.
- **Leftovers on the server:** the failed backup left a partial folder, `/var/backups/scalesmiths/pre-empower-20261121T090025Z-4c399b8`. I'll delete it when the server is back.
- **CI on master:** it is now green on `37995d2`. The one failure was a flaky login test, and re-running it passed. The same code had passed on the PR, and the test fails only when login happens to land on the Command Centre page.
- **Why the backup failed:** the migration database account isn't allowed to read one table, `client_analytics_audit_logs`, because of a row-level access rule. I've changed the backup script to run as the server's local `postgres` admin account instead, which needs no password. Once the server is back, the plan is unchanged: backup, then 22 migrations, then build the release, then switch over the two live apps, then smoke checks. All four Empower switches stay off.

**Security: please rotate this password.** When the backup failed, the error message printed the full database connection string, including the `scalesmiths_migration` password, into this session's transcript. I'd change that password and update `.env` on the server. I haven't done this myself.

**Backup limits:** this backup stays on the server and isn't encrypted. The proper backup process from the release runbook needs three tools (age, rclone and jq) that aren't installed there.

content.content:
SHA=<full-40-char-git-sha>
RELEASE_TREE="$(dirname "$CANONICAL_CHECKOUT")/releases/$SHA"
```

`$RELEASE_TREE` resolves to the sibling release directory of the canonical checkout (layout: `…/ScaleSmiths` and `…/releases/<sha>/`).

## Prepare a release tree

Sync the approved checkout into a new immutable release directory (exclude build artefacts, secrets, and generated sites):

```bash
cd "$CANONICAL_CHECKOUT"
git fetch origin
git checkout --detach "$SHA"

rsync -a --delete \
  --exclude node_modules \
  --exclude .next \
  --exclude .env \
  --exclude generated-sites \
  "$CANONICAL_CHECKOUT"/ "$RELEASE_TREE"/

# Reuse the protected host env; do not rsync secrets from laptops.
cp -a "$CANONICAL_CHECKOUT/.env" "$RELEASE_TREE/.env"

cd "$RELEASE_TREE/web" && npm ci && npm run build
cd "$RELEASE_TREE/admin" && npm ci && npm run build
```

Confirm both apps produced `.next` output before touching PM2.

## Cut over PM2 (one-line starts)

`pm2 restart` against an old `cwd` will not pick up a new tree or a new `SS_RELEASE_ID`. Delete and recreate so both `cwd` and env change. Prefer single-line starts (no shell line-continuations that operators paste incompletely):

```bash
pm2 delete scalesmiths-web-canary
pm2 start bash --name scalesmiths-web-canary --cwd "$RELEASE_TREE/web" -- -lc "export SS_RELEASE_ID=$SHA; exec node --env-file-if-exists=../.env ./node_modules/next/dist/bin/next start -H 127.0.0.1 -p 3200"

pm2 delete scalesmiths-admin-canary
pm2 start bash --name scalesmiths-admin-canary --cwd "$RELEASE_TREE/admin" -- -lc "export SS_RELEASE_ID=$SHA; exec node --env-file-if-exists=../.env ./node_modules/next/dist/bin/next start -H 127.0.0.1 -p 3201"

pm2 save
```

If discovery shows different loopback ports, use those ports instead of 3200/3201 — do not guess against Nginx.

## Verify

```bash
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:3200/api/health
curl -sS https://scalesmiths.co.uk/api/health
pm2 show scalesmiths-web-canary
pm2 show scalesmiths-admin-canary
```

Expect `release` to equal `$SHA`. Spot-check public routes from the [release runbook](release-runbook.md) smoke list.

## Rollback

Keep the previous SHA tree on disk. Recreate both PM2 apps with `cwd` and `SS_RELEASE_ID` pointed at the previous tree and the same ports, then `pm2 save` and re-check health.

content.text:
Operation Empower B1.1–B1.4 (commit `37995d2`) is now live on production, and all checks passed. All four Empower switches are off, so nothing new is visible to founders or partners yet.

**What ran**
1. **Server after the outage:** it wasn't rebooted (238 days' uptime), all PM2 apps were online and there were no out-of-memory events, so it looks like a network outage.
2. **Backup:** `/var/backups/scalesmiths/pre-empower-20261121T090150Z-4c399b8`. It contains a full database dump taken as the local `postgres` account, the migration journals, PM2 and nginx config, and SHA256SUMS.
3. **Release build:** I created `/var/www/scalesmiths/releases/37995d2…` from git and built web and admin there.
   - I left the old checkout at `4c399b8` untouched so it can be rolled back to.
   - The new release's `generated-sites` folder is a link to the existing one, so the Forge workspaces (625 MB) stay shared rather than copied.
4. **Migrations:** 0073–0094 applied cleanly; the database now has admin 95/95 and web 24/24.
5. **Switchover:** web went first and was checked before admin; PM2 is saved.
6. **Checks:**
   - Both health endpoints report release `37995d2` with the database OK.
   - These public pages return 200: `/`, `/faq`, `/partners`, `/api/health`, and the admin login.
   - Partner pages redirect anonymous visitors to the login page (307), and the partner APIs refuse them (401).
   - A release note with the rollback steps is saved in the backup folder.

**Still open**
- **Rotate the migration password.** The `scalesmiths_migration` password was exposed in this session's transcript earlier, so please change it and update the server's `.env`.
- **Forge dead-letter queue:** admin logged that 7 Forge jobs are in the dead-letter queue. That's a warning and has nothing to do with this release.
- **Backup is local only:** it's on the server and not encrypted, because the tools the runbook needs (age, rclone and jq) aren't installed there.
- **Old process unchanged:** the megaton worker still runs from its older release, `6dcfeff`, as before.
- **Flaky CI test:** the Forge login test in CI looks for any navigation menu on the page. It clashes with the Command Centre's tabs when login lands there, which is why master CI failed once and then passed on a re-run. It's worth fixing separately.
- **Nothing is approved or enabled:** content still needs founder approval in the studio before any switch is turned on.

/** Partner sign-in lives on the existing admin origin; no separate partner subdomain or auth stack. */
export function partnerLoginUrl(env: { NEXT_PUBLIC_ADMIN_URL?: string; NODE_ENV?: string } = process.env as never): string {
  const configured = env.NEXT_PUBLIC_ADMIN_URL?.trim()
  let base = env.NODE_ENV === "production" ? "https://admin.scalesmiths.co.uk" : "http://localhost:3103"
  if (configured) { try { const url = new URL(configured); if (["http:", "https:"].includes(url.protocol) && !url.username && !url.password) base = url.origin } catch { /* keep default */ } }
  return `${base}/login`
}

/** Partner sign-in lives on the existing admin origin; no separate partner subdomain or auth stack. */
export function partnerLoginUrl(env: { NEXT_PUBLIC_ADMIN_URL?: string; NODE_ENV?: string } = process.env as never): string {
  const configured = env.NEXT_PUBLIC_ADMIN_URL?.trim()
  let base = env.NODE_ENV === "production" ? "https://admin.scalesmiths.co.uk" : "http://localhost:3103"
  if (configured) { try { const url = new URL(configured); if (["http:", "https:"].includes(url.protocol) && !url.username && !url.password) base = url.origin } catch { /* keep default */ } }
  return `${base}/login`
}

questions.question: The partner and founder logins are one app with one fixed auth origin (AUTH_URL = admin.scalesmiths.co.uk), and Auth.js redirects plus CSRF origin checks all use it. Should partners.scalesmiths.co.uk become that single origin for everyone (founders sign in there too), or should founders stay on admin.* while partners use partners.*?

options.label: partners.* for everyone (Recommended)
options.description: Env-only change: AUTH_URL, NEXT_PUBLIC_ADMIN_URL and ADMIN_PORTAL_URL become https://partners.scalesmiths.co.uk; nginx 301s admin.* to partners.*. Web gets rebuilt so its links change. No code change.

options.label: Two origins
options.description: Founders keep admin.*, partners use partners.*. Needs a code change to allow a list of origins in middleware and the CSRF checks, plus tests, a PR and a redeploy of admin. Slower.

content.text:
The fix needs one change in Cloudflare, which only you can make: the `partners` and `admin` DNS records point at a different server, apparently the confirmakill one. The ScaleSmiths server never receives that traffic.

**How I know**
- On our server, `admin.scalesmiths.co.uk/login` returns the login page (200).
- Through Cloudflare, both hosts end up at a different nginx that redirects to `www.confirmakill.co.uk`. A test file I placed on our server never showed up in its access log.
- Let's Encrypt failed for the same reason, so I couldn't issue the certificate yet.

**In Cloudflare DNS, for the scalesmiths.co.uk zone:**
- Set `partners` to an A record pointing at `185.242.225.178`, proxied (orange cloud), the same as the root record.
- Set `admin` to the same.

**Done on the server so far**
- **Nginx:** a new site config for `partners.scalesmiths.co.uk` that sends traffic to the admin app on 3201.
  - It answers on ports 80 and 443 and can serve the Let's Encrypt challenge.
  - Until the real certificate exists, it borrows the `admin` certificate; Cloudflare will accept that only if its SSL mode isn't "Full (strict)".
  - The config passed `nginx -t` and nginx has been reloaded.
- **Repo:** commit `6a0311b` on branch `fix/partner-login-origin` changes the Partner Login default to `https://partners.scalesmiths.co.uk/login`, with its test (6 tests pass) and two docs. It is not pushed yet.

**Not done yet**
- The site's Partner Login links will keep pointing at `admin.scalesmiths.co.uk` until the switch below.
- I've deliberately held back switching the admin app's sign-in address from `admin.*` to `partners.*`: changing it before partners.* actually reaches our server would break sign-in. It's three settings in `.env` (`AUTH_URL`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_ADMIN_URL`, `ADMIN_PORTAL_URL`).

**Once the records are fixed**
1. Issue the certificate and swap it into the partners config.
2. Back up `.env`, switch the three settings to `https://partners.scalesmiths.co.uk`, and restart admin.
3. Rebuild web and restart it, because `NEXT_PUBLIC_ADMIN_URL` is fixed when web is built. That rebuild is what changes the Partner Login button and the footer link.
4. Test sign-in end to end on `partners.scalesmiths.co.uk`.

content.text:
The Partner Login links now go to `https://partners.scalesmiths.co.uk/login`. That covers all 5 on `/partners` (hero button, apply section and footer) and the footer link on the home page. The partners site shows the sign-in form over a valid certificate. I haven't signed in with a real account, so a sign-in on your side would confirm the whole flow.

**Changes on the server**
- **Nginx:** the `scalesmiths-partners` site answers on port 80 (certificate checks, otherwise redirect to HTTPS) and port 443 (passes everything to the admin app). It now uses its own Let's Encrypt certificate, which renews through the same folder.
- **Sign-in address:** `AUTH_URL`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_ADMIN_URL` and `ADMIN_PORTAL_URL` now point to the partners site. I changed them in the live release's `.env`, in the main checkout's `.env` and in the megaton worker's `.env`. Each file has a timestamped `.bak-` copy beside it.
- **Admin and worker:** both restarted. Sign-in redirects now send people to the partners site.
- **Web:** rebuilt in a separate folder and switched over, so the public site stayed up throughout. The previous `web/` build is kept for rollback.
- **Record:** all of this is added to the release note in the backup folder.

**Still open**
- **admin.scalesmiths.co.uk** still redirects to confirmakill in Cloudflare. Either the record hasn't been changed, or a Cloudflare redirect rule is doing it. It doesn't matter for signing in any more, but anything that still calls `admin.*` from outside (for example monitoring or bookmarks) will hit confirmakill until it's fixed.
- **Founders sign in at partners.scalesmiths.co.uk too.** Emails from the web app now link there, as does the admin app's own address setting.
- **Repo commit `6a0311b`:** without it, a future build with no `NEXT_PUBLIC_ADMIN_URL` set would fall back to `admin.*`. The commit makes partners.* the default, updates the test and two docs, and isn't pushed yet.

input.content:
## Summary

Partner Login on the public site pointed at `admin.scalesmiths.co.uk/login`, which Cloudflare sends to another origin (confirmakill). By founder decision, the admin app's single canonical origin is now `https://partners.scalesmiths.co.uk` for partners and founders alike. This changes the production fallback of `partnerLoginUrl()` and its test, and updates two docs. The live value still comes from `NEXT_PUBLIC_ADMIN_URL`, which production already sets to the partners origin.

## Type

- [ ] `feat`
- [x] `fix`
- [x] `test`
- [x] `docs`
- [ ] `refactor`
- [ ] `security`
- [ ] `perf`
- [ ] `chore`

## Scope

- [x] Public web
- [ ] Admin
- [ ] Forge
- [ ] Database/migrations
- [ ] Docker/deployment/Nginx
- [ ] CI/tooling
- [ ] Documentation only

## Validation

Commands run, with results:

```text
web: vitest run src/lib/partner-programme.test.ts -> 6 passed
Production (already applied on the host, outside this PR):
  https://scalesmiths.co.uk/partners -> 5 links to https://partners.scalesmiths.co.uk/login
  https://partners.scalesmiths.co.uk/login -> 200, sign-in form, valid certificate
  /partner/academy on partners host -> 307 to https://partners.scalesmiths.co.uk/login
```

Commands not run, and why:

```text
Full web suite, typecheck and build not run locally for this two-line change; CI runs them.
```

## Migrations

- [x] No database migration.
- [ ] Migration included and documented below.

## Environment

- [x] No environment-variable change.
- [ ] Environment variables added to `.env.example` and documented below.

Production `.env` values for `AUTH_URL`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_ADMIN_URL` and `ADMIN_PORTAL_URL` were changed on the host to `https://partners.scalesmiths.co.uk`; no new variable.

## Security and Privacy

- [x] No secrets, provider credentials, real `.env` files, database dumps, or
      client-private exports are included.
- [x] Admin/Forge access control and generated-workspace isolation are preserved.
- [x] Public analytics remains minimised and consent-aware.

## Evidence

Host changes recorded in the pre-Empower release note on the server: nginx `scalesmiths-partners` vhost, Let's Encrypt certificate for the partners host, env switch, rebuilt web canary.

## Residual Risk and Follow-up

- `admin.scalesmiths.co.uk` still resolves through Cloudflare to another origin; anything calling `admin.*` from outside needs updating or the Cloudflare record fixing.
- Founders now sign in at the partners host.

## Rollback

Revert this commit. On the host, restore the `.env.bak-<timestamp>` files and restart the canaries.

I've pushed the branch and opened [TheFridey/ScaleSmiths#158](https://github.com/TheFridey/ScaleSmiths/pull/158) against `master`. CI hasn't reported any checks yet.

The PR changes the code's default Partner Login address to `https://partners.scalesmiths.co.uk/login`, updates its test (6 pass locally), and updates two docs. It also records the server changes and how to roll them back.

The live site already uses the partners address from the server's settings, so merging changes nothing visible. It only matters for a future build where that setting is missing; without this PR, that build would point the link back at `admin.*`.

Still open outside the PR: `admin.scalesmiths.co.uk` still redirects to confirmakill in Cloudflare. Anything that calls `admin.*` from outside, like monitoring or bookmarks, will land on confirmakill until that record or redirect rule is fixed.

<pasted_content id="831a">
OPERATION LAUNCH READY
ScaleSmiths — Production Engineering, Partner Onboarding, Agreements, Approval Gates & Premium UX
You are acting as the Principal Software Engineer, Product Designer, Security Engineer, QA Lead and Release Engineer for ScaleSmiths Limited.
Your assignment is to bring the ScaleSmiths website, administration platform and international partner onboarding experience to a professional, production-ready standard.
This is an implementation assignment, not a research-only exercise.
You must inspect the existing systems, identify deficiencies, implement appropriate improvements, test your changes and produce verifiable evidence.
Do not stop after completing an audit. Do not repeatedly ask what to work on next. Continue through the workstreams in dependency order, making safe engineering decisions within the boundaries below.
1. SYSTEMS AND CONTEXT
Company: ScaleSmiths Limited
Repository: https://github.com/TheFridey/ScaleSmiths
Relevant production services:

* https://scalesmiths.co.uk
* https://partners.scalesmiths.co.uk
* Existing ScaleSmiths administration application
* https://app.scalesmiths.co.uk — ScaleSmiths Connect

Infrastructure includes Next.js, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Nginx and Linux VPS deployments. Verify actual versions, service names, architecture and deployment methods before acting.
The company is building an international network of independent sales partners who introduce businesses to ScaleSmiths services.
The partner programme must support application review, contractual onboarding, training, lead management, commissions, milestones, performance visibility and ongoing communication.
ScaleSmiths already has substantial functionality. Extend and improve the existing architecture; do not replace working systems unnecessarily.
Other agents may be working on the repository concurrently. Inspect active branches, commits, pull requests, working trees and deployments before making changes.
2. NON-NEGOTIABLE ENGINEERING RULES

1. Inspect the actual repository and production state. Never assume an earlier report is still accurate.
2. Read existing architecture documents, contribution guidance, security policies and deployment procedures.
3. Use an isolated feature branch. Never overwrite another agent's uncommitted work.
4. Prefer small, reviewable commits with descriptive messages.
5. Do not expose secrets, credentials, tokens or personal information in logs, reports or commits.
6. Never modify production databases destructively.
7. Use reversible migrations with verified backups and rollback procedures.
8. Never bypass legal, commercial, founder or security approval gates.
9. Never activate unfinished partner features simply to demonstrate them.
10. Do not deploy automatically unless deployment is explicitly authorised and all release gates pass.
11. Do not manufacture test results or mark incomplete features as finished.
12. Avoid placeholder functionality, fake data presented as real, dead buttons and cosmetic-only fixes.
13. Preserve existing brand identity and functionality.
14. Continue independently through all safe, authorised development work rather than repeatedly requesting permission.

If blocked by an external approval, document the blocker, keep the feature safely disabled and continue with independent tasks.
3. PHASE ONE — FULL PRODUCTION AND CODEBASE AUDIT
Before changing application code, establish a verified baseline.
Repository inspection
Inspect:

* Public website architecture
* Partner application architecture
* Administration application
* Authentication and authorisation
* Partner database schema
* Application and approval workflows
* Agreement/document infrastructure
* Commission and milestone logic
* Feature flags
* Email delivery
* Background jobs
* Audit logging
* API routes
* Error handling
* CI/CD and deployment workflows
* Existing tests and coverage

Identify duplicated functionality, unfinished implementations, dead code, inconsistent UI components and unsafe assumptions.
Production investigation
Using authorised VPS access, investigate:

* Application service health
* Recent server and application errors
* Nginx errors and upstream failures
* Failed API requests
* Database connection errors
* Authentication failures
* Unhandled exceptions
* Deployment-related failures
* Missing environment configuration
* Background job failures
* Email delivery failures
* Browser console errors
* Client-side hydration errors

Distinguish genuine defects from harmless warnings, expected authentication redirects and historical errors.
Do not indiscriminately clear logs.
Deliverable
Create a baseline report containing:

* Verified architecture
* Currently deployed commits
* Active feature flags
* Confirmed defects
* Reproduction steps
* Severity
* Root causes where established
* Proposed fixes
* Relevant test coverage
* Deployment risks

Then proceed immediately to implementation.
4. PHASE TWO — COMPLETE PARTNER ONBOARDING
The objective is a coherent, secure, professional experience from initial application to fully activated independent sales partner.
Application lifecycle
Audit and implement the appropriate lifecycle:
Application received → Under review → Additional information required / Rejected / Conditionally approved → Agreement pending → Agreement accepted → Founder approval complete → Account activated → Onboarding in progress → Active partner
Adapt this lifecycle to the existing system rather than introducing unnecessary duplicate states.
Ensure transitions are enforced server-side.
Founder administration
Founders should be able to:

* View applicants in a clear, searchable directory
* Filter by status, country, submission date and review state
* Inspect applicant information
* Record internal review notes
* Request additional information
* Approve or reject applications
* Issue approved agreement versions
* Monitor agreement acceptance
* Complete mandatory approval steps
* Activate eligible accounts
* Suspend or revoke access
* View a complete audit history

Design an efficient workflow with minimal unnecessary navigation.
Use meaningful status indicators, clear actions and confirmation dialogs for consequential decisions.
Applicant experience
Applicants should receive:

* Professional application confirmation
* Clear next-step communications
* Secure access to outstanding onboarding tasks
* A readable agreement review experience
* Explicit acceptance controls
* Clear explanations of pending approvals
* Account activation instructions
* Appropriate error and recovery states

Do not expose internal founder notes or confidential administrative information.
Partner first-login experience
After activation, the partner should encounter a polished onboarding experience.
Include, where appropriate:

* Welcome dashboard
* Onboarding progress
* Profile completion
* Agreement status
* Required training
* Academy access
* Resource Centre
* Knowledge Base
* Lead submission guidance
* Commission structure
* Milestone progression
* Support and communication access

Existing feature flags and commercial approval requirements must remain enforced.
Do not expose unfinished modules.
Email communications
Review the existing email infrastructure.
Implement or repair transactional communications for appropriate lifecycle events, with:

* Consistent ScaleSmiths branding
* Clear subjects
* Responsive layouts
* Correct sender identity
* Safe links
* No confidential information leakage
* Retry and failure handling
* Idempotency where needed
* Auditability

Test delivery safely without sending unintended emails to real applicants.
5. PHASE THREE — PARTNER AGREEMENTS
Build or complete a secure, versioned agreement workflow.
Important: Software implementation is authorised. Legal drafting, commercial approval and publication of binding terms are not automatically authorised.
Do not invent legally binding terms or declare documents legally compliant without appropriate review.
Agreement requirements
The system should support:

* Draft agreement templates
* Explicit document versions
* Founder approval before publication
* Immutable published versions
* Assignment of an approved version to an applicant
* Full agreement review before acceptance
* Explicit affirmative acceptance
* Acceptance timestamp
* Authenticated account identity
* Exact accepted document version
* Document content hash
* Tamper-evident audit history
* Downloadable accepted agreement
* Founder visibility
* Reissue when an agreement changes
* Appropriate withdrawal and supersession workflows

Assess whether the existing system supports electronic signing adequately or whether an external e-signature provider is required.
Do not claim legal equivalence between a simple checkbox and a compliant electronic-signature process.
Commercial terms
Respect the existing independent sales partner model.
The current advertised structure includes 30% commission on eligible initial sales payments, but the authoritative approved commercial specification must be identified before implementing calculations or publishing contractual language.
Do not assume that advertised commission terms alone define:

* Eligibility
* Payment timing
* Refunds
* Chargebacks
* Cancellations
* Tax treatment
* Territory rights
* Exclusivity
* Termination
* Disputes
* Governing law

Identify unresolved commercial decisions and place them behind explicit founder approval.
Agreement security
Ensure:

* Partners cannot alter agreement versions
* Published versions cannot be silently edited
* Acceptance cannot be backdated
* Acceptance cannot be forged by client-side requests
* Partners cannot accept agreements for other users
* A revoked agreement cannot activate an account
* Superseded agreements follow explicit policy
* Audit records cannot be silently deleted

Write regression tests for these conditions.
6. PHASE FOUR — FOUNDER APPROVAL GATES
This is a critical security and governance requirement.
Approval must be enforced in the backend, not merely represented by disabled buttons.
Mandatory principles

* No application activation without required approvals
* No agreement publication without appropriate approval
* No access to restricted partner resources before eligibility
* No commission entitlement without the applicable verified conditions
* No cross-partner access to private information
* No unauthorised founder impersonation
* No approval by users lacking the correct role
* No silent approval when a dependency fails
* No bypass through direct API requests
* No duplicate approval or activation from retries

Governance
Where multiple founders must approve an action, implement the established approval policy.
Do not invent a new voting or commercial governance structure.
Review the existing B1.1–B1.4 founder-content, Academy, Resources and Knowledge workflows and their feature flags.
Preserve their existing safeguards.
Auditability
Every consequential action should record:

* Actor
* Target
* Action
* Previous state
* New state
* Timestamp
* Relevant document or policy version
* Reason where required

Sensitive audit information must be accessible only to authorised personnel.
Testing
Create negative tests for:

* Unauthorised approvals
* Missing agreements
* Expired or withdrawn invitations
* Duplicate submissions
* Replay attempts
* Invalid state transitions
* Cross-tenant access
* Direct API bypasses
* Concurrent approval races
* Suspended accounts
* Revoked permissions

Fail closed when a mandatory approval cannot be verified.
7. PHASE FIVE — PREMIUM WEBSITE AND PARTNER UX
ScaleSmiths should feel like a polished, established international technology company.
The visual standard should be comparable to high-quality modern SaaS platforms, not a generic template or unfinished internal dashboard.
Brand
Preserve the official ScaleSmiths identity:

* Metallic interlocking S emblem
* Silver and gold wordmark
* Premium dark presentation where appropriate
* Restrained gold accents
* Professional typography
* Consistent visual hierarchy

Use existing authoritative brand assets. Do not redraw or reinterpret the logo.
Public website
Audit and improve:

* Header and navigation
* Hero sections
* Service pages
* Calls to action
* Mobile menus
* Contact forms
* Partner recruitment journey
* Trust and credibility sections
* Footer
* Loading behaviour
* Performance
* SEO fundamentals
* Accessibility
* Error pages

Ensure every CTA leads somewhere meaningful.
Partner dashboard
Improve:

* Navigation and information architecture
* Dashboard overview
* Applicant/onboarding status
* Member and profile views
* Lead management
* Commission visibility
* Milestone tracking
* Training and resources
* Settings
* Notifications
* Empty states
* Error states
* Confirmation dialogs

Prioritise clarity and ease of use over decorative complexity.
Animation and interaction
Introduce polished, purposeful interactions:

* Responsive hover states
* Smooth panel transitions
* Subtle card elevation
* Clear active and selected states
* Button press feedback
* Loading skeletons
* Success confirmations
* Error feedback
* Dropdown animations
* Modal transitions
* Keyboard focus indicators

Animations should feel responsive and premium.
Avoid excessive movement, distracting effects and sluggish transitions.
Support `prefers-reduced-motion`.
Mobile quality
Test realistic device widths, including approximately:

* 390px
* 768px
* 1024px
* 1440px

Verify touch targets, mobile keyboards, forms, navigation, scrolling, modals and content overflow.
Accessibility
Target WCAG 2.2 AA where practicable.
Check:

* Keyboard navigation
* Visible focus
* Accessible names
* Colour contrast
* Form labels
* Error announcements
* Semantic structure
* Screen-reader usability
* Reduced motion

Do not sacrifice accessibility for visual effects.
8. PHASE SIX — PRODUCTION ERROR REMEDIATION
Treat error remediation as an engineering workstream, not a log-clearing exercise.
For each confirmed production error:

1. Capture a safe reproduction.
2. Identify the affected service.
3. Determine severity and user impact.
4. Trace the underlying cause.
5. Implement the smallest robust correction.
6. Add regression coverage.
7. Verify the fix in a safe environment.
8. Document deployment and rollback requirements.

Prioritise authentication, onboarding, agreements, approvals, data integrity and broken customer-facing functionality.
Observability
Improve visibility into:

* Unhandled exceptions
* API failure rates
* Authentication failures
* Background job failures
* Email delivery failures
* Database failures
* Deployment regressions

Use structured logs and correlation identifiers where appropriate.
Do not log passwords, access tokens, agreement secrets or unnecessary personal information.
Evaluate external alerting, but do not introduce paid services or transmit production data to new providers without approval.
9. PHASE SEVEN — COMPREHENSIVE TESTING
Testing must cover actual behaviour, not simply successful compilation.
Automated checks
Run relevant:

* TypeScript checks
* Linting
* Unit tests
* Integration tests
* Database migration tests
* Production builds
* Security regressions
* Browser end-to-end tests

Browser testing
Use Playwright or the repository's established browser tooling.
Test real application journeys.
Cover:

* Mouse interactions
* Hover states
* Buttons
* Links
* Dropdowns
* Forms
* Modals
* Keyboard navigation
* Mobile layouts
* Validation errors
* Loading states
* Empty states
* Network failures
* Session expiration

Capture screenshots at relevant breakpoints.
Inspect console errors and failed network requests.
Do not claim complete coverage merely because a script hovered over buttons.
Multi-role testing
Test using appropriately isolated accounts representing:

* Founder
* Applicant
* Pending partner
* Active partner
* Suspended partner
* Unauthorised visitor

Verify both permitted actions and denied actions.
Use synthetic or isolated test data.
Never create unintended real commissions, send real applicant emails or alter genuine agreements during testing.
Acceptance criteria
The operation is not complete until:

* Critical onboarding journeys pass
* Approval gates are enforced server-side
* Agreement version integrity is demonstrated
* Unauthorised access tests pass
* Relevant production errors are resolved or documented
* No known critical browser regressions remain
* Builds and CI checks pass
* A safe rollback procedure exists
* Unresolved legal/commercial approvals remain explicitly gated

10. RELEASE MANAGEMENT
Prepare the implementation for production without assuming deployment permission.
Before release:

* Identify exact target commit
* Confirm clean working tree
* Verify CI
* Review migrations
* Confirm backup availability
* Document rollback
* Check feature flags
* Check pending legal approvals
* Confirm no secrets were introduced

Do not modify production agreement records or enable unapproved commercial functionality.
If deployment is authorised, use the established release process and verify production after deployment.
Never declare deployment successful solely because a process restarted.
11. REQUIRED DELIVERABLES
Create or update suitable repository documentation covering:
A. Baseline audit

* Current architecture
* Deployed state
* Defects and risks

B. Implementation changelog

* Files changed
* Features added
* Defects fixed
* Migrations
* Commits

C. UX review

* Before/after findings
* Screenshots
* Responsive results
* Accessibility findings

D. Partner onboarding report

* Lifecycle
* Permissions
* Agreement workflow
* Approval gates
* Email notifications

E. Test evidence

* Commands executed
* Pass/fail counts
* Browser coverage
* Known limitations

F. Release-readiness report

* Ready features
* Disabled features
* Outstanding approvals
* Remaining blockers
* Deployment instructions
* Rollback instructions

Open a pull request when the implementation is ready for review, if repository permissions permit.
12. EXECUTION STRATEGY
Work in the following order:

1. Verify repository and production baseline.
2. Fix critical production errors affecting onboarding and authentication.
3. Complete partner application lifecycle.
4. Complete agreement versioning and acceptance.
5. Enforce founder approval gates.
6. Integrate onboarding communications and first-login experience.
7. Perform the premium public website and partner dashboard visual pass.
8. Complete accessibility and responsive improvements.
9. Run comprehensive regression testing.
10. Resolve failures and repeat tests.
11. Prepare the final pull request and release-readiness report.

Keep changes coherent and avoid unnecessary architectural rewrites.
Do not stop after writing a plan. Execute the plan.
Do not stop after the first successful test.
Do not declare an incomplete workflow complete.
Do not ask for confirmation between ordinary, reversible engineering tasks.
Where a legal, financial, security or production-release decision requires founder authorisation, preserve the gate, record the blocker and continue other work.
FINAL OBJECTIVE
Deliver a ScaleSmiths platform that is visually premium, technically robust and ready for controlled international partner onboarding.
The finished experience must make applicants confident in the company, make partners understand exactly what they need to do next, and give founders complete visibility and control over applications, agreements and approvals.
Build it, verify it, document it and prepare it for release. Do not substitute a roadmap for implementation.
Begin by inspecting the repository and actual production state now.
